passage:
Hafsa had spent the weekend drafting what to say. On Monday she knocked on Tarun's open door. "Do you have ten minutes? I want to do good work here. Could you show me exactly what needs work, and could corrections come privately when you can?" Her voice was steady; her hands were not. When Sudha asked at the tea point whether she had complained to anyone, Hafsa shook her head. "I'd rather ask him."

Tarun stared at his screen afterwards and replayed the meeting. He had assumed she already knew the standard. He had also read out her mistake in front of six people. Both things were true. "You're right about the second part," he told her the next day. "The total was wrong and still needs fixing. But I should have told you privately, and I should have shown you the standard first." Hafsa let out a long breath.

They agreed on ten minutes every Thursday and a one-page list of what a finished report looks like. In the weeks after, Hafsa asked a question the moment she was unsure. Once she said, "I see that wording differently," and Tarun answered, "Good, tell me why." Saying things out loud cost less than the evenings of rehearsing.

qa.q: How often did Hafsa and Tarun agree to meet?
qa.a: They agreed to meet for ten minutes every Thursday.

qa.q: How did Hafsa's choice not to complain to others and Tarun's reflection lead to the new working norms?
qa.a: Hafsa asked calmly for a private talk instead of venting to peers, which made Tarun replay the meeting and admit he had assumed she knew the standard and had corrected her in front of six people, while the total still needed fixing. That led to the Thursday ten minutes and a one-page list.

qa.q: How was Hafsa feeling as she knocked on Tarun's door?
qa.a: She felt nervous but determined: her voice was steady though her hands were not.

qa.q: Why was it wise that Tarun kept the content of his correction while owning how he said it?
qa.a: It told her the total still needed fixing so she could improve, while respecting her dignity, which made honest talk safe.

grounding: Shows the later workplace conflict stages: an intern's calm request for private feedback, the senior reflecting on his manner, and agreed working norms.
